Paraumbilical defect is characteristic of gastroschisis, usually to the right of the umbilicus.
Exposed bowel lacks the membranous sac typical of omphalocele.
Fluid and heat loss are major early concerns.
Bowel assessment is important because intestinal complications may coexist.

title: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome: Pathophysiology, Signs and Symptoms, Diagnosis and Treatment

notes.text: It happen mainly as an adverse effect to typical and atypical antipsychotic drugs, but it also occur after sudden discontinuation of antiparkinsonian drugs
Life threatening condition with mortality rate of 20%
It is a set of symptoms
Signs and symptoms
Patient develop NMS within hours to days after exposure to causative medication
Initially present as muscle rigidity
Then fever develops because sweating is impaired in these patients due to the anticholinergic effects of antipsychotics
Stress leukocytosis starts
Stress leukocytosis and fever may mislead you into thinking it is infectious process but it is not
Altered mental status: confused or stuporous patient
Autonomic instability in form of altered blood pressure and heart rate is present
Muscle creatine kinase is elevated reflecting muscle damage
Tachypnea, tachycardia, sialorrhea, flushing, skin pallor and incontinence maybe present
Other extrapyramidal mtoor findings (other than rigidity) maybe present like tremor, chorea, akinesia and dystonia
Other symptoms include dysphagia, dyspnea, abnormal reflexes, mutism and seizures
This syndrome occurs due to excessive blocking of dopamine receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway by the antipsychotic medications administered to the patient
This lead to severe form of extrapyramidal symptoms in form of NMS

With sudden discontinuation of antiparkinsonian drugs, there is already dopamine receptor upregulation but dopamine suddenly decreased which gives the same dopamine deficiency thus leading to severe extrapyramidal symptoms in form of NMS
Main risk factors include
Use of high potency antipsychotics
Rapid increase in the dose of the antipsychotic medications
The use of long acting forms of antipsychotics (e.g. intramuscular depot)
Concomitant use of lithium
NMS diagnosed according to DSM IV criteria
In DSM IV criteria for NMS, there should be:
Altered mental status (from confusion to coma)
Change in blood pressure
Elevated creatine phosphokinase in lab testing
Differential diagnosis
Status epilepticus
Neurologic emergency
Stopping the antipsychotic medication or if it happen when withdrawing an antiparkinsonian medication then put the patient on that medication again quickly
Aggressive hydration to prevent renal failure due to rhabdomyolysis
Diazepam used to as a muscle relaxant
Metabolic abnormalities should be corrected
Cooling of the patient body to relieve fever
The patient might require hemodialysis to solve the renal failure occurred from rhabdomyolysis
Switching to atypical antipsychotic drug is indicated after the syndrome resolved
Renal failure secondary to rhabdomyolysis
DIC secondary to rhabdomyolysis
Venous thromboembolism from dehydration and immobilization
Aspiration pneumonia because of the altered mental status and difficulty swallowing
Cardiopulmonary failure

Central cyanosis reflects reduced arterial oxygenation or abnormal hemoglobin rather than isolated peripheral vasoconstriction.
Cardiac disease and pulmonary disease are major diagnostic categories.
Preductal and postductal saturations can provide useful physiologic clues.
Perfusion assessment is essential because cyanosis and shock may coexist.

title: Buprenorphine: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Buprenorphine is a synthetic opioid, working as a mixed agonist/antagonist (partial agonist).
Synthesized in the late 1960s, it is a derivative of thebaine.
Famous for its use in the treatment of pain and opioid misuse disorder.
Pharmacokinetics
Available in sublingual, buccal, transdermal, IV, and IM formulations.
Oral formula is not used due to significant first pass effect.
Bioavailability: sublingual 30%, buccal 65%.
Metabolized by the liver (CYP3A4 and CYP2C8).
Onset of action: 30 minutes after administration.
Elimination half-life: ~37 hours; duration of action: ~20 hours.
Excreted through kidney and liver.
Mechanism of Action
Acts as a potent partial agonist at mu opioid receptor and antagonist at kappa and delta receptors (mixed agonist antagonist).
Compared to morphine for equivalent dose, buprenorphine sublingual is ~50 times more potent, and 100 times more potent as a transdermal patch.
Can displace full mu agonists (e.g., morphine) due to higher potency, leading to withdrawal symptoms in opioid-dependent patients.
Pharmacologic Effect
Provides analgesia for moderate to severe pain, but can antagonize the analgesic effects of agonist opioids if used concurrently.
Less euphoric effects, thus lower abuse potential than agonist opioids.
Lower risk of respiratory depression compared to agonist opioids.
Slow dissociation from receptors leads to long duration of action and mild withdrawal symptoms when stopped.
Therapeutic Uses
Treatment of chronic pain (as transdermal patch), with long duration (~24 hours).
Treatment of opioid addiction (like methadone) due to long duration, less withdrawal symptoms, and blocking effects of agonist opioids during effect period.
Shorter and less severe withdrawal symptoms compared to methadone.
For opioid misuse disorder, used in combination with naloxone sublingually or buccally; IV use is avoided to prevent abuse (naloxone would cause acute withdrawal if injected).
Does not cause respiratory depression unless at very high dose, but if it occurs, it cannot be reversed by naloxone.
Risk of respiratory depression is higher if injected IV with benzodiazepines.
Increased blood pressure due to increased systemic and pulmonary vascular resistance.
Prolongation of QT interval (risky in cardiovascular diseases).
Psychotomimetic effects: hallucinations, nightmares, anxiety (reported with mixed agonist-antagonist drugs).
Low addiction risk due to less mu activation.
Nausea and vomiting.
Headache, mild amnesia, cognitive and neural inhibition.
Risk of seizures in epilepsy patients.
Urinary retention.
